verses.zh: 约伯接着说：
verses.en: And Job took up his discourse again:[NOTE:1]
notes: The Hebrew word מָשָׁל (mashal) is characteristically “proverb; by-word.” It normally refers to a brief saying, but can be used for a discourse (see A. R. Johnson, “Mašal,” VTSup 3 [1955]: 162ff.).

verses.zh: 神夺去我的理，全能者使我心中愁苦。我指着永生的　神起誓：
verses.en: “As surely as God lives,[NOTE:1] who has denied me justice,[NOTE:2] the Almighty, who has made my life bitter[NOTE:3]—
notes: The expression חַי־אֵל (khay ʾel) is the oath formula: “as God lives.” In other words, the speaker is staking God’s life on the credibility of the words. It is like saying, “As truly as God is alive.”
“My judgment” would here, as before, be “my right.” God has taken this away by afflicting Job unjustly (A. B. Davidson, Job, 187).
The verb הֵמַר (hemar) is the Hiphil perfect from מָרַר (marar, “to be bitter”) and hence, “to make bitter.” The object of the verb is “my soul,” which is better translated as “me” or “my life.”

verses.zh: 我的生命尚在我里面；　神所赐呼吸之气仍在我的鼻孔内。
verses.en: for while[NOTE:1] my spirit[NOTE:2] is still in me,and the breath from God is in my nostrils,
notes: The adverb עוֹד (ʿod) was originally a noun, and so here it could be rendered “all the existence of my spirit.” The word comes between the noun in construct and its actual genitive (see GKC 415 §128.e).

The word נְשָׁמָה (neshamah) is the “breath” that was breathed into Adam in Gen 2:7. Its usage includes the animating breath, the spiritual understanding, and the functioning conscience—so the whole spirit of the person. The other word in this verse, רוּחַ (ruakh), may be translated as “wind,” “breath,” or “spirit/Spirit” depending on the context. Here, since it talks about the nostrils, it should be translated “breath.”

verses.zh: 我的嘴决不说非义之言；我的舌也不说诡诈之语。
verses.en: my[NOTE:1] lips will not speak wickedness,and my tongue will whisper[NOTE:2] no deceit.
notes: The verse begins with אִם (ʾim), the formula used for the content of the oath (“God lives…if I do/do not…”). Thus, the content of the oath proper is here in v. 4.
The verb means “to utter; to mumble; to meditate.” The implication is that he will not communicate deceitful things, no matter how quiet or subtle.

verses.zh: 我断不以你们为是；我至死必不以自己为不正！
verses.en: I will never[NOTE:1] declare that you three[NOTE:2] are in the right;until I die, I will not set aside my integrity!
notes: The text uses חָלִילָה לִּי (khalilah li) meaning “far be it from me,” or more strongly, something akin to “sacrilege.”
In the Hebrew text “you” is plural—a reference to Eliphaz, Zophar, and Bildad. To make this clear, “three” is supplied in the translation.

verses.zh: 我持定我的义，必不放松；在世的日子，我心必不责备我。
verses.en: I will maintain my righteousnessand never let it go;my conscience[NOTE:1] will not reproach mefor as long as I live.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “my heart.”
The prepositional phrase “from my days” probably means “from the days of my birth,” or “all my life.”

verses.zh: 愿我的仇敌如恶人一样；愿那起来攻击我的，如不义之人一般。
verses.en: “May my enemy be like the wicked,[NOTE:1] my adversary[NOTE:2] like the unrighteous.[NOTE:3]
notes: Of course, he means like his enemy when he is judged, not when he is thriving in prosperity and luxury.
The form is the Hitpolel participle from קוּם (qum): “those who are rising up against me,” or “my adversary.”
The LXX made a free paraphrase: “No, but let my enemies be as the overthrow of the ungodly, and they that rise up against me as the destruction of transgressors.”

verses.zh: 不敬虔的人虽然得利，　神夺取其命的时候还有甚么指望呢？
verses.en: For what hope does the godless have when he is cut off,[NOTE:1] when God takes away his life?[NOTE:2]
notes: The verb יִבְצָע (yivtsaʿ) means “to cut off.” It could be translated transitively or intransitively—the latter is better here (“when he is cut off”). Since the next line speaks of prayer, some have thought this verse should be about prayer. Mandelkern, in his concordance (p. 228b), suggested the verb should be “when he prays” (reading יִפְגַּע [yifgaʿ] in place of יִבְצָע [yivtsaʿ]).
The verb יֵשֶׁל (yeshel) is found only here. It has been related spoils [or sheaves]”); שָׁאַל (shaʾal, “to ask”); נָשָׂא (nasaʾ, “to lift up” [i.e., pray]); and a host of others.

verses.zh: 患难临到他，　神岂能听他的呼求？
verses.en: Does God listen to his crywhen distress overtakes him?

verses.zh: 他岂以全能者为乐，随时求告　神呢？
verses.en: Will he find delight[NOTE:1] in the Almighty?Will he call out to God at all times?
notes: See the note on 22:26 where the same verb is employed.

verses.zh: 神的作为，我要指教你们；全能者所行的，我也不隐瞒。
verses.en: I will teach you[NOTE:1] about the power[NOTE:2] of God;what is on the Almighty’s mind[NOTE:3] I will not conceal.
notes: The object suffix is in the plural, which gives some support to the idea Job is speaking to them.
Heb “the hand of.”
Heb “[what is] with Shaddai.”

verses.zh: 你们自己也都见过，为何全然变为虚妄呢？
verses.en: If you yourselves have all seen this,Why in the world[NOTE:1] do you continue this meaningless talk?[NOTE:2]
notes: The interrogative uses the demonstrative pronoun in its emphatic position: “Why in the world…?” (IBHS 312-13 §17.4.3c).

The text has the noun “vain thing; breath; vapor,” and then a denominative verb from the same root: “to become vain with a vain thing,” or “to do in vain a vain thing.” This is an example of the internal object, or a cognate accusative (see GKC 367 §117.q). The LXX has “you all know that you are adding vanity to vanity.”

verses.zh: 神为恶人所定的分，强暴人从全能者所得的报（原文是产业）乃是这样：
verses.en: This is the portion of the wicked man allotted by God,[NOTE:1] the inheritance that evildoers receive from the Almighty.
notes: The expression “allotted by God” interprets the simple prepositional phrase in the text: “with/from God.”

verses.zh: 倘或他的儿女增多，还是被刀所杀；他的子孙必不得饱食。
verses.en: If his children increase—it is for the sword![NOTE:1] His offspring never have enough to eat.[NOTE:2]
notes: R. Gordis (Job, 294) identifies this as a breviloquence. Cf. Ps 92:8 where the last two words also constitute the apodosis.
Heb “will not be satisfied with bread/food.”

verses.zh: 他所遗留的人必死而埋葬；他的寡妇也不哀哭。
verses.en: Those who survive him are buried by the plague,[NOTE:1] and their[NOTE:2] widows do not mourn for them.
notes: The text says “will be buried in/by death.” A number of passages in the Bible use “death” to mean the plague that kills (see Jer 15:2; Isa 28:3; and BDB 89 s.v. ב 2.a). In this sense it is like the English expression for the plague, “the Black Death.”
The LXX has “their widows” to match the plural, and most commentators harmonize in the same way.

verses.zh: 他虽积蓄银子如尘沙，预备衣服如泥土；
verses.en: If he piles up silver like dustand stores up clothing like mounds of clay,

verses.zh: 他只管预备，义人却要穿上；他的银子，无辜的人要分取。
verses.en: what he stores up[NOTE:1] a righteous man will wear,and an innocent man will inherit his silver.
notes: The text simply repeats the verb from the last clause. It could be treated as a separate short clause: “He may store it up, but the righteous will wear it.” But it also could be understood as the object of the following verb, “[what] he stores up the righteous will wear.” The LXX simply has, “All these things shall the righteous gain.”

verses.zh: 他建造房屋如虫做窝，又如守望者所搭的棚。
verses.en: The house he builds is as fragile as a moth’s cocoon,[NOTE:1] like a hut[NOTE:2] that a watchman has made.
notes: Heb כָעָשׁ (khaʿash, “like a moth”), but this leaves room for clarification. Some commentators wanted to change it to “bird’s nest” or just “nest” (cf. NRSV) to make the parallelism; see Job 4:14. But the word is not found. The LXX has a double expression, “as moths, as a spider.” So several take it as the spider’s web, which is certainly unsubstantial (cf. NAB, NASB, NLT; see Job 8:14).
The Hebrew word is the word for “booth,” as in the Feast of Booths. The word describes something that is flimsy; it is not substantial at all.

verses.zh: 他虽富足躺卧，却不得收殓，转眼之间就不在了。
verses.en: He goes to bed wealthy, but will do so no more.[NOTE:1] When he opens his eyes, it is all gone.[NOTE:2]
notes: The verb is the Niphal יֵאָסֵף (yeʾasef), from אָסַף (ʾasaf, “to gather”). So, “he lies down rich, but he is not gathered.” This does not make much sense. It could mean “he will not be gathered for burial,” but that does not belong here. Many commentators accept the variant יֹאסִף (yoʾsif) stood for יוֹסִיף (yosif, “will [not] add”). This is what the LXX and the Syriac have. This leads to the interpretive translation that “he will do so no longer.”

Heb “and he is not.” One view is that this must mean that he dies, not that his wealth is gone. R. Gordis (Job, 295) says the first part should be made impersonal: “when one opens one’s eyes, the wicked is no longer there.” E. Dhorme (Job, 396) has it more simply: “He has opened his eyes, and it is for the last time.” But the other view is that the wealth goes overnight. In support of this is the introduction into the verse of the wealthy. The RSV, NRSV, ESV, and NLT take it that “wealth is gone.”

verses.zh: 惊恐如波涛将他追上；暴风在夜间将他刮去。
verses.en: Terrors overwhelm him like a flood;[NOTE:1] at night a whirlwind carries him off.
notes: Many commentators want a word parallel to “in the night.” And so we are offered בַּיּוֹם (bayyom, “in the day”) for כַמַּיִם (khammayim, “like waters”) as well as a number of others. But “waters” sometimes stand for major calamities, and so may be retained here. Besides, not all parallel structures are synonymous.

verses.zh: 东风把他飘去，又刮他离开本处。
verses.en: The east wind carries him away, and he is gone;it sweeps him out of his place.

verses.zh: 神要向他射箭，并不留情；他恨不得逃脱　神的手。
verses.en: It hurls itself against him without pity[NOTE:1] as he flees headlong from its power.
notes: The verb is once again functioning in an adverbial sense. The text has “it hurls itself against him and shows no mercy.”

verses.zh: 人要向他拍掌，并要发叱声，使他离开本处。
verses.en: It claps[NOTE:1] its hands at him in derisionand hisses him away from his place.[NOTE:2]
notes: If the same subject is to be carried through here, it is the wind. That would make this a bold personification, perhaps suggesting the force of the wind. Others argue that it is unlikely that the wind claps its hands. They suggest taking the verb with an indefinite subject: “he claps” means “one claps. The idea is that of people rejoicing when the wicked are gone. But the parallelism is against this unless the second line is changed as well. R. Gordis (Job, 296) has “men will clap their hands…men will whistle upon him.”
Or “hisses at him from its place” (ESV).
